title: From starlight to a radial-velocity time series
boundary: This guide explains high-resolution stellar Doppler work. It does not treat every astronomical spectrograph as a precision-RV instrument.

steps.title: Record a spectrum
steps.plain_language: A spectrograph spreads starlight by wavelength. Dark absorption lines form a repeatable pattern, but the recorded pattern is also shaped by the atmosphere, telescope, fibre, optics and detector.
steps.technical_note: Resolving power is R = lambda / delta-lambda. It describes separation of nearby wavelengths; it is not the same quantity as radial-velocity accuracy.

steps.title: Attach a wavelength reference
steps.plain_language: Known reference features connect detector pixels to wavelength and reveal instrumental drift. The reference may be imprinted on the stellar beam or recorded through a second fibre.
steps.technical_note: Iodine-cell modelling solves the wavelength scale and line-spread function in each exposure. Stabilized instruments may instead combine ThAr, Fabry-Perot and laser-comb information.
steps.source_label: Butler et al. (1996); ESO ESPRESSO QC

steps.title: Extract a relative shift
steps.plain_language: Software compares the observed line pattern with a mask or a high-signal template. The measured displacement is a relative Doppler shift, not yet a planet measurement.
steps.technical_note: Cross-correlation compresses many lines into a mean profile. Template matching fits more of the pixel-level spectrum. Both depend on masking, weights, interpolation and outlier decisions.

steps.title: Remove the observer's motion
steps.plain_language: Earth rotates and orbits while the exposure is being taken. A barycentric correction transforms the measured shift to a reference frame centred on the Solar System barycentre.
steps.technical_note: Centimetre-per-second work requires relativistic terms, accurate coordinates and timing, and photon-weighted exposure information. A geometric exposure midpoint can be insufficient.

steps.title: Interpret a time series
steps.plain_language: A planet can create a repeating stellar reflex signal, but spots, faculae, oscillations, convection, tellurics and instrumental changes can also move or reshape spectral lines.
steps.technical_note: A Keplerian semi-amplitude depends on period, planet mass, stellar mass, inclination and eccentricity. Radial velocity usually constrains M sin(i), not the true mass by itself.
steps.source_label: NASA Exoplanet Archive; Dumusque et al. (2017)

techniques.name: Iodine absorption cell
techniques.reference_path: Reference and stellar lines share the same beam.
techniques.what_it_solves: Models wavelength, instrumental profile and Doppler shift for each exposure.
techniques.tradeoff: The iodine forest occupies a limited optical range and must be disentangled from the stellar spectrum.

techniques.name: Simultaneous reference fibre
techniques.reference_path: Star and calibrator use separate fibres and are recorded together.
techniques.what_it_solves: Tracks spectrograph drift during the science exposure.
techniques.tradeoff: The calibrator does not perfectly share the stellar optical path, so fibre illumination and transfer errors remain.
techniques.example: HARPS simultaneous ThAr or Fabry-Perot modes

techniques.name: Stabilized spectrograph plus template matching
techniques.reference_path: A stable wavelength solution supports comparison to a high-signal stellar template.
techniques.what_it_solves: Uses the observed spectrum directly instead of reducing every line to one binary-mask profile.
techniques.tradeoff: Template construction, telluric masking, interpolation and stellar variability can still bias the result.

taxonomy.typical_scale: High resolving power, controlled illumination and stability designed for repeated stellar Doppler measurements.

taxonomy.class_name: General high-resolution spectrograph with RV work
taxonomy.typical_scale: Can support radial-velocity studies, but its design and operating modes serve a broader spectroscopy programme.
Gaia RVS has R about 11,500 and measures many millions of stars, with km/s-scale performance depending on magnitude and spectral type.
NIRSpec spans 0.6–5.3 micrometres at R about 100, 1,000 or 2,700 for galaxy, stellar-population and exoplanet-atmosphere spectroscopy.

equations.name: Small Doppler shift
equations.expression: Delta lambda / lambda approximately equals v_r / c
equations.meaning: A line pattern shifted by a tiny fraction of its wavelength corresponds to a line-of-sight velocity. Precision comes from combining information across many pixels and lines.

equations.name: Resolving power
equations.meaning: R describes spectral resolution. Sub-pixel modelling of many lines can measure shifts much smaller than one resolution element, but accuracy still depends on calibration and stability.

equations.name: Photon-limited uncertainty
equations.meaning: In the Bouchy et al. formulation, Q represents the Doppler information in the spectrum and N_e is the detected photoelectron count. This is a statistical floor, not a complete long-term error budget.

comparators.name: Gaia RVS
comparators.why_here: A useful example of a space radial-velocity survey, but not an extreme-precision exoplanet spectrograph.
comparators.fact: R approximately 11,500 over 845–872 nm; Gaia DR3 contains median radial velocities for about 33 million stars.

comparators.name: JWST NIRSpec
comparators.why_here: A useful example showing that the word spectrograph covers instruments built for very different measurements.
comparators.fact: 0.6–5.3 micrometres and R approximately 100, 1,000 or 2,700 across four observing modes.
